Let me analyze these teaching examples carefully to identify systematic errors in the forecasts compared to true outcomes.

Looking at Example 1 (2024-06-25):
- History shows prices drifting lower from ~75 to ~67.5 over 18 days
- Model forecasts are also generally lower but seem to lag or don't capture the magnitude well
- Looking at the first 10 days of the 30-day forecast vs outcome:
  - Day 1: Model 67.77 vs True 67.80 (close)
  - Day 5: Model 68.63 vs True 68.33 (model overestimates by ~0.30)
  - Day 10: Model 69.86 vs True 68.52 (model overestimates by ~1.34)
  - Day 15: Model 68.27 vs True 67.94 (overestimates by ~0.33)
  - Day 20: Model 66.28 vs True 65.79 (overestimates by ~0.49)
  - Day 25: Model 70.70 vs True 68.78 (overestimates by ~1.92)

Wait, let me look at this differently. The model forecasts appear to be based on a linear regression on the history. Let me check if the error has a systematic pattern.

Looking at Example 5 (2024-08-21) - this is interesting because it's after Example 4:
- History: prices are generally higher now (72-78 range)
- Model forecasts: also higher, but seem to overestimate
- Day 1: Model 72.50 vs True 72.14 (+0.36)
- Day 5: Model 73.02 vs True 71.49 (+1.53)
- Day 10: Model 71.99 vs True 68.16 (+3.83)


- Day 15: Model 71.67 vs True 66.52 (+5.15)
- Day 20: Model 70.72 vs True 63.21 (+7.51)
- Day 25: Model 72.47 vs True 64.10 (+8.37)

I notice a consistent pattern of model overestimation, particularly in the later days. The divergence grows larger as we extend further into the forecast, suggesting the model struggles to accurately predict price movements when extrapolating beyond the immediate historical data.

The sentiment analysis reveals a nuanced relationship.
